claims.text: Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films have a high density of grain boundaries.
A high density of grain boundaries accelerates oxygen diffusion in CuMoTaWV films.
Accelerated oxygen diffusion produces rapid and continuous passive oxide-film formation.
Rapid and continuous passive oxide-film formation mitigates both mechanical wear and corrosive degradation.
Coarse-grained CuMoTaWV films have less grain-boundary area available for oxygen diffusion than nanocrystalline films.
Magnetron sputtering followed by controlled annealing can produce nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films suitable for comparison with coarse-grained films.
Grain boundaries serve as rapid oxygen-diffusion pathways that catalyze formation and repair of a protective passive oxide film.
Faster oxygen ingress in nanocrystalline films leads to more uniform passive-film formation under simultaneous tribological and corrosive attack.
Rapid passive-film repair reduces localized film breakdown.
Reduced localized film breakdown maintains a barrier against mechanical abrasion and corrosive attack.
Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films will have lower friction coefficients than matched coarse-grained films.
Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films will have lower wear volumes than matched coarse-grained films.
Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films will have lower corrosion current densities than matched coarse-grained films.
The performance advantage of nanocrystalline films will be greatest under intermittent wear conditions that allow passive-film healing.
The advantage of nanocrystalline films may diminish under constant extreme wear when damage overwhelms passive-film regeneration.
Coarse-grained CuMoTaWV films form passive films more slowly and are more susceptible to localized corrosion and wear.
The proposed benefit should hold in moderate-to-severe corrosive environments under cyclic wear that permits passive-film reformation.
Excessive mechanical stress or microcracking may eliminate the nanocrystalline film's performance benefit.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and XPS mapping can assess passive-oxide formation and its distribution at grain boundaries during the proposed comparison.
Failure to observe enhanced passive-film formation or statistically different wear and corrosion performance in nanocrystalline films would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
